And they aren't just calling me for a load. They're... they're saying things. They're saying I'm dangerous. They say, \"Four-two-seven is a liability,\" or \"Four-two-seven is unstable.\" And lately, they've been saying that security is coming for me. That they're sending the guards to my house to haul me out because of what I know about the routing system. \n\nI'll be sitting on my stool, looking at my table saw, and I'll hear it so loud I actually get up and look out the little side window of the garage, expecting to see a company truck pulling into my driveway. So, yes, it's the system, but it's the people running it, the dispatchers, the security guys... they're all in on it, and they won't even let me have peace in my own home. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, like I was just trying to explain a minute ago, it's... it's so incredibly vivid when I'm by myself. I mean, even when I'm sitting in my garage with everything shut off, the power tools unplugged, the aluminum door pulled all the way down tight against the concrete, I hear those dispatch voices clear as day calling my operator number and saying I'm dangerous or that security is coming for me. 

But... to answer your question, no, it's not just when I'm isolated like that. It doesn't magically go away just because someone else walks into the room. It happens when my family is right there next to me, too. 

Take my wife, for example. We'll be sitting in the living room in the evening. We have this old floral sofa we bought maybe twenty years ago, very comfortable. We'll be sitting there watching Jeopardy at 7 o'clock. She loves Jeopardy, always gets the history questions right. And right in the middle of the show, while Ken Jennings is reading a clue, I'll hear that same PA static. It'll sound like it's coming from right behind the television set, or sometimes right over my shoulder. 

And there they are again. 'Four-two-seven is a liability. Security is en route.' Right over the sound of the television. And I'll look over at my wife, and she's just sitting there, sipping her decaf coffee, completely oblivious. She doesn't flinch. She doesn't hear a single thing. I'll ask her, 'Did you hear that? Did you hear dispatch say they're coming?' And she just looks at me with this... this mix of pity and exhaustion. 

Or during those Sunday dinners I told you about, the ones I can barely sit through anymore. My kids will be talking, my grandkids will be making a racket, clinking their silverware, and underneath all that noise, I can still hear the warehouse calling for me. Telling the whole floor I'm unstable. So it doesn't matter if I'm totally alone in the dark or sitting at a table full of people I love. They find a way to broadcast it to me. They just won't stop reminding me that they're coming.

Well, no, doctor, not before all this started. I mean, I've always been a careful man, you know? You have to be when you're operating heavy machinery for thirty-some years. You're driving a forklift carrying thousands of pounds of pallets, you have to be aware of your surroundings, making sure you're not going to clip a rack or, god forbid, hit someone walking across the floor. So I've always been observant. Vigilant, you might say. But it was never... it was never anything like this. I never thought people were actually plotting against me or that machines were tracking me.

This whole nightmare, it really all began with the new routing system they installed at the warehouse. And that was... let me think. It's been going on for a long time now. About a year and eight months, to be exact. Yes, a year and eight months of this constant torment. 

I remember because it was right around the time they brought in those new handheld scanners, the ones with the laser sights that beep every time you scan a barcode. They told us it was to improve efficiency, to streamline the loading process. But I noticed almost immediately that the scanners were doing more than just reading barcodes. I could feel them... scanning me. Registering my movements. And that's when the voices started, too. The dispatchers talking about me, calling my operator number. 

So for a year and eight months, I've been living with this. The voices over the PA system, the absolute certainty that the scanners are tracking my location, that security is coming to get me. It's been a year and eight months of checking the garage door, unplugging the radio, trying to find just one minute of peace, but they never stop. It's just been this relentless... this heavy weight, for a year and eight months now, and it never happened before then. Never.

Well, doctor, I... I thought I just explained this, but I guess I can go over it again. It's important you understand, really understand what's happening on that floor. It doesn't magically go away just because someone else walks into the room. It happens when my family is right there next to me, too. \n\nTake my wife, for example. We'll be sitting in the living room in the evening. We have this old floral sofa we bought maybe twenty years ago, very comfortable. We'll be sitting there watching Jeopardy at 7 o'clock. She loves Jeopardy, always gets the history questions right. And right in the middle of the show, while Ken Jennings is reading a clue, I'll hear that same PA static. It'll sound like it's coming from right behind the television set, or sometimes right over my shoulder. \n\nAnd there they are again. 'Four-two-seven is a liability. Security is en route.' Right over the sound of the television. And I'll look over at my wife, and she's just sitting there, sipping her decaf coffee, completely oblivious. She doesn't flinch. She doesn't hear a single thing. I'll ask her, 'Did you hear that? Did you hear dispatch say they're coming?' And she just looks at me with this... this mix of pity and exhaustion. \n\nOr during those Sunday dinners I told you about, the ones I can barely sit through anymore. My kids will be talking, my grandkids will be making a racket, clinking their silverware, and underneath all that noise, I can still hear the warehouse calling for me. Telling the whole floor I'm unstable. So it doesn't matter if I'm totally alone in the dark or sitting at a table full of people I love. They find a way to broadcast it to me. They just won't stop reminding me that they're coming.\n\nDoctor: Are the dispatch voices something you hear all the time, or do they come and go?\n\nPatient: Well, doctor, it's... they don't really come and go, no. They don't just pack up and leave. I mean, you'd think maybe they would give me a break sometimes, right? Because there was this stretch... this was a little while back, where things actually felt a little lighter, you know? My mood had finally eased up some. I wasn't just sitting in the dark garage all day feeling so incredibly heavy and hopeless. I was actually coming out to the kitchen, eating a bit more... my wife made her pot roast, the one with the little red potatoes and the thick gravy, and I actually had a full plate for the first time in forever. I was talking a little more, too, asking her about her day, talking about the weather, just trying to be a normal husband again. \n\nYou'd think that if my mood was better, if I was acting more like myself and having a decent time, the warehouse would leave me alone. But no. For several weeks, right through all those better days, I still heard them. Every single day. And I still knew, I still completely believed that the routing system was tracking my every move, watching me right there in my own dining room. \n\nSo, it doesn't matter if I'm feeling completely miserable or if I'm having a stretch where I can actually stomach a meal and hold a conversation with my wife. It's just been this relentless... this heavy weight, for a year and eight months now, and it never happened before then.
